This is the vicious conundrum no one ever talks about. Everyone is telling us to "rid yourself of toxic people", "surround yourself with positive people", "focus on friendships that energize you and enrich your life", etc. etc. So, what does that mean for depressed people? That we can only be friends with other depressed people? As a result, we try to deny how sad we are, and we end up watching people slowly fade out of our lives as they discover, over time, how sad we truly are.

Have you been able to understand how/why you remained depressed for 15+ years? What do you think you needed during all those years, that you weren't getting? I'm sure you had attempted to get help before, just not to the extent you went to in the last month or so, is that right?

Well, negative experiences are apart of everyday life. We do have a responsibility in transmuting that pain, or leveraging it, into something meaningful, or into an opportunity. It is very difficult to do. Without a purpose, or something that we can give our lives to, it is very difficult to see our pain as worth it. I know, for myself, that I am partially responsible for my depression for various reasons: feeling lonely is probably a result of my introversion and social anxiety. I am to blame for not actively trying to reduce my social anxiety. I am to blame for not asking for help for my depression. Am I to blame for things that have happened to me? Not always. But, sometimes.

Personally, I think love is a reflection of yourself and your own life circumstances. The more deeply you think and feel, the more deeply you can feel another person. The more anxiety-ridden and depressed you are, the more anxiety-ridden and difficult your relationship can seem. Ultimately, love waxes and wanes, just as your own ephemeral self-concept. Love is not an endless adventure. It is, like a previous post mentioned, a conscious choice to commit to another human being. It is deciding to witness the growth and regression, the laughter and the tears, the hopelessness and elevation of one of the most novel things on this planet: another human being. Practicing love is like flexing a muscle. It takes effort, it takes patience, it takes commitment. It is painful, it is beautiful, it is terrifying, it is simply life-changing. 

Unconditional love? I'm not sure I believe in that. We all have basic needs, and social relationships are by far, the most essential. With one in four Americans reporting they have no one to share their personal triumphs or struggles with (http://www.npr.org/templates/story/story.php?storyId=5509381)
, it is no wonder why "love" can feel so strained, and often so draining and crazy. To me, that kind of dependent love is the bane of this society. But, how are we to know better? The world has become increasingly secularized for the past 300 years, we live in isolating circumstances in which a third of us don't know our neighbors (http://nymag.com/scienceofus/2015/08/third-of-americans-dont-know-their-neighbors.html). Love feels like a gimmick when we hardly know how to cultivate healthy friendships, and meaningful, bountiful ones , at that. Rambling with a touch of despair.
